title: Real, fake — or something in between?
summary: What makes a forgery, how museums grade authorship, and why honest uncertainty is part of the job.

shots.title:
Real, fake —
or in between?
shots.subtitle: Authenticity is rarely a **yes-or-no** question.
shots.narration: Is this painting real? It sounds like a yes-or-no question. In the art world it almost never is — and that gap is exactly where forgers work.

shots.text: A forgery is made or sold **to deceive**. A copy or a student's study is not — until someone lies about it.
shots.narration: What makes a fake is intent. Curators treat the intent to deceive as central, and the motives vary: money, wounded pride, a wish to fool the experts, a need for attention.

left.heading: Honest
items: A 'genuine fake', signed by the copyist

shots.narration: The same brushstrokes can be honest or fraudulent. John Myatt, once jailed for forgery, now sells 'genuine fakes', clearly signed so they can never pass as originals.

shots.heading: Between 'by' and 'not by'
shots.narration: Museums grade authorship. 'By' means reasonable certainty; 'attributed to' signals doubt; 'studio', 'follower' and 'imitator' step further and further from the master's own hand.

shots.text: Old workshops were teams. A **workshop piece** can be genuinely old — and still not by the master.
shots.narration: Renaissance painters ran workshops with apprentices and assistants. A picture by the chief assistant is a genuine old painting — just not an autograph one, painted entirely by the master.

shots.text: The Getty dates its marble youth **'about 530 B.C. or modern forgery'**.
shots.footnote: J. Paul Getty Museum, Kouros, accession 85.AA.40
shots.narration: Sometimes even the owner cannot decide. The Getty Museum labels its marble kouros 'about 530 B.C. or modern forgery': experts have never resolved it.
Forgers follow the money. When an artist's prices rise, or a major study is published, previously unknown works tend to surface — a pattern collectors are warned to watch.
We start with looking, then materials, then the forgers themselves. You'll practise every detection method in labs, survey the field today, and finish with your own authentication dossier.

shots.text: Every claim has a **source** and a **date**. Where experts disagree, you'll see the **disagreement**.
shots.narration: One rule throughout: every fact is sourced and dated, and where experts disagree you'll see the disagreement, not a tidy story. Look in the margin for the evidence.

steps.title: Forgery, honest work or open question?
steps.brief: Sort each case. What matters is not how good the work is, but whether anyone set out to deceive — and whether the question is actually settled.

cards.text: A life-size Cupid, buried and aged so that it would sell in Rome as an ancient sculpture.
cards.why: Vasari reports it was sold to a cardinal as an antique. The deception makes it a fake — even though, by his account, Michelangelo carved it.

cards.text: A Van Gogh–style canvas, clearly signed by the copyist and sold as his own work.
cards.why: John Myatt's 'genuine fakes' are signed so they can never be sold as authentic.

cards.text: A marble statue its museum catalogues as 'about 530 B.C. or modern forgery'.
cards.why: The Getty says neither art historians nor scientists have resolved the kouros's authenticity.

cards.text: An old portrait catalogued as 'studio of' a famous master.
cards.why: A workshop piece is a genuine period painting; the label honestly says a pupil probably painted it.

cards.text: Fake 'old masters' given to museums as gifts, in memory of a parent.
cards.why: Mark Landis's gifts were forgeries — though, as nobody paid him, he technically committed no fraud.

cards.text: A painting on which two AI systems disagree: one says Raphael, one says not.
cards.why: The de Brécy Tondo split two AI models in 2023; neither result settles the attribution.

questions.prompt: What turns a skilful copy into a forgery?
options: The intent to deceive when it is made or sold
questions.explain: Copies, pastiches and studies are legitimate. Curators treat the intent to deceive as central to fakes.

questions.prompt: Order these labels from most to least certain about the master's own hand.
questions.explain: 'Attributed to' signals doubt; 'studio of' means a pupil under direction; a 'follower' only admired the style.

questions.prompt: The Getty catalogues its kouros as 'about 530 B.C. or modern forgery'. What does that tell you?
options: The museum has proved it fake
The museum has proved it ancient
Experts have not resolved its authenticity
It is a copy of a lost statue
questions.explain: The Getty states that neither art historians nor scientists have completely resolved the question — an honest label.
